metadata.title: Claude, Unstuck
metadata.subtitle: Troubleshooting and Staying Current
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: when a plugin breaks, does the fix live in the screenshot or in the concept? Explain the machinery — five durable failure shapes and a four-step diagnostic loop — and judge the ecosystem trade-off that dates the interface while leaving the mental model intact. Lands the carry-out: return to what the plugin is for, then check the docs for what's current.

beats.narration_text: Things break — plugin misbehaves, connection drops, output disappoints. Here's what's actually at stake — not the bug, but the failure mode where frustration accumulates until you quietly stop reaching for the tool. Diagnosing is the counter-move that keeps you in the game.

production_viz.label: FRUSTRATION, NOT THE BUG
production_viz.caption: diagnosing keeps you in the game

beats.narration_text: Here's the discipline. The interface — buttons, menus, wording — churns constantly because product teams optimize for polish and iteration. Underneath sits something durable: what the plugin is actually for, what it can and can't do. Troubleshoot from there.

Here's what's actually happening — most breakage collapses into five shapes: won't appear, won't authenticate, results feel generic, runs slow, or a command isn't recognized. Each has a durable cause underneath the specific error text, and a durable fix that outlives the current UI.

Plugin missing after you installed it? Here's the mechanism — plugins load once at app startup, not continuously. A mid-session install sits on disk but isn't registered until the next boot. Close the app completely, reopen it, and it loads. Still missing? Reinstall from the sidebar.

A service that won't authenticate — almost always stale credentials. Tokens expire on a schedule, passwords rotate, access gets revoked when someone leaves. The fix is a fresh handshake: disconnect the service, then reconnect. If your company gates outside access, you'll need IT to sign off before the loop closes.

Results feel generic? That's not a bug — that's the design. Defaults are deliberately broad so the plugin ships useful to everyone, specific to nobody. Feed it your context: brand voice, process, standards. The output sharpens well past the useful threshold — once it has something to specialize on.

Slow operations almost always reach outside your machine — a database lookup, a web search, a CRM query. Each buys network latency you can't optimize away because the roundtrip isn't local. Here's the fix: shrink the scope. One date range, one folder, not everything everywhere.

A slash command not recognized? Here's what's actually happening — the command list is registered by active plugins only. Confirm the plugin is installed and enabled, then type a single slash to see everything available right now. Still missing? Restart it — the registry rebuilds on load.

Two diagnostics run first — cheap and high-yield. Check the plugins list to see what's installed and active; it's the opening move for anything plugin-related. If one's misbehaving, disable it, then re-enable it. That forces a fresh config load and clears most transient glitches.

Then the loop that resolves most problems, in a specific order. One: is the plugin installed and active? Two: are its connections authorized? Three: try a simpler request to isolate where it fails. Four: restart. The order matters — most trouble dies inside those four steps.

That third step carries more weight than its size suggests. Shrink the request until it works, then grow it back one dimension at a time. The exact point it breaks again is a bisection — it names precisely where the problem lives.

production_viz.label: ISOLATE BY SHRINKING
production_viz.caption: the break point is the diagnosis

beats.narration_text: Plugins don't sit still. Anthropic improves the official ones on their release cadence; community creators ship their own updates whenever they're ready. Each release can add capabilities, fix bugs, or run faster — so what you learned last month may behave differently today.

production_viz.label: NOTHING SITS STILL
production_viz.caption: what you learned may already differ

beats.narration_text: And that's the catch. Updates apply automatically, so the interface shifts underneath you — freshness optimized at the expense of stability. Anything written down about the screen starts dating the moment it's written. The concept underneath does not.

production_viz.label: THE SCREEN DATES
production_viz.caption: written screenshots age; the concept doesn't

beats.narration_text: So verify specifics against sources that stay current. Each plugin's own docs — on its page and inside the app, the authoritative source. The plugin directory, where others have already worked through your problem. And the official channels — the Anthropic blog and release notes — for what actually changed.

Make it a habit. Set a monthly reminder to browse the directory — the ecosystem moves whether you're watching or not. When a plugin you rely on changes, read the changelog: a new feature might be exactly what you were missing, or the workaround you were building around.

production_viz.label: A MONTHLY HABIT
production_viz.caption: a new feature might be the fix

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt — paste it into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I'm learning to troubleshoot AI plugins from the concept up, not from a specific screenshot. Walk me through the five most common failure modes — won't appear, won't authenticate, results feel generic, runs slow, and command not recognized. For each one, explain the durable underlying cause, give me the first check to run, and name the design trade-off that made this failure mode possible. Then hand me a four-step diagnostic loop I can run on any plugin issue in any product, in the order I should run it. Go deeper: which of these failure modes is most likely to get worse — not better — as plugin ecosystems mature and add community contributors, and why? Liam, in for Bear.
